chapters.title: Chapter 4: Deep Learning Foundations for Market Sequences

lessons.title: 1D CNNs for Pattern Recognition in OHLCV Data

body.text: A 1D CNN treats a price window the way an image classifier treats a photo: scanning for a specific local shape that could appear anywhere in the frame, using far fewer parameters than an LSTM with a comparable field of view. Given this chapter's opening warning about capacity and thin signal, that parameter efficiency alone is often reason enough to try a CNN before reaching for recurrence.

children.text: The Core Idea: A Learned Filter Sliding Across Time

A 1D convolution slides a small filter of length k across the time dimension of a sequence, computing a weighted sum at every position, with the same filter weights reused everywhere. That weight sharing is what lets it detect a pattern, three down days followed by a volume spike, say, regardless of where in the window it occurs, directly solving the problem the previous lesson raised about flattened feedforward inputs. It also processes every position in the window in parallel rather than stepping through them one at a time, which is why a CNN typically trains noticeably faster than an LSTM of comparable capacity.
Receptive Field: How Far Back a CNN Can 'See'

markDefs.definition: The number of input time steps a given output position in a convolutional network actually depends on. A single layer's receptive field equals its kernel size; stacking layers, especially with dilation, expands it further.

children.text: A single convolutional layer with kernel size k only sees k consecutive time steps. Stacking layers expands the

, and using dilated convolutions, skipping over inputs at a fixed spacing, expands it far faster per layer than stacking plain convolutions would. Doubling the dilation rate at each successive layer is the trick WaveNet (van den Oord et al., 2016) popularized for modeling long audio sequences without recurrence, and the same idea applies just as well to a price sequence.

body.caption: For L stacked convolutional layers, each with kernel size kₗ and dilation dₗ. With dilation doubling at each layer (1, 2, 4, 8, ...), receptive field grows exponentially with depth instead of linearly, reaching a long effective memory with far fewer layers than a plain, undilated stack would need.

children.text: Causal Convolutions: No Peeking at Future Time Steps

A standard convolution is centered: its output at position t depends on input positions both before and after t within the kernel's width. Apply that unchanged to a time series and the output for a given date depends partly on days after it, a leak in the same family as every other look-ahead problem this course has flagged since Chapter 1, just hiding inside a default padding argument this time. The fix is a causal convolution: pad only on the left, the past, so the output at position t depends only on input positions at or before t, never later.

body.text: PyTorch's Conv1d with padding="same" pads symmetrically by default, centered, not causal. Used directly on a price sequence ending at the prediction date, this quietly lets future time steps leak into the prediction, exactly the kind of subtle, framework-default leak this course keeps surfacing in new places. Always pad left-only, manually, for a causal convolution.

body.caption: Padding left by (kernel_size − 1) × dilation, then applying Conv1d with no further padding, guarantees the output at every position depends only on that position and earlier ones.

body.code:
import torch

class CNNSignal(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_channels, num_filters=16, dropout=0.3):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv1 = CausalConv1d(input_channels, num_filters, kernel_size=3, dilation=1)
        self.conv2 = CausalConv1d(num_filters, num_filters, kernel_size=3, dilation=2)
        self.drop = nn.Dropout(dropout)
        self.fc = nn.Linear(num_filters, 1)

    def forward(self, x):
        # x arrives as (batch, time, channels); Conv1d wants (batch, channels, time)
        x = x.transpose(1, 2)
        x = F.relu(self.conv1(x))
        x = F.relu(self.conv2(x))
        last_step = x[:, :, -1]        # most recent time step's learned features
        out = self.drop(last_step)
        return torch.sigmoid(self.fc(out)).squeeze(-1)
body.caption: Two dilated causal layers (dilation 1, then 2) give a receptive field of 1 + 2×1 + 2×2 = 7 time steps, per this lesson's formula, from just 16 filters per layer, deliberately small for the same reason the previous lesson kept its LSTM's hidden size small.

children.text: CNN vs LSTM: Which One, and When

body.caption: Neither is a strict upgrade over the other

cells: Fast; all time steps processed in parallel
Slower; must step through the sequence one position at a time
Parameters for a given field of view
Can need more parameters to reach comparable effective memory
Fixed-length local patterns that can occur anywhere in the window
Variable-length dependencies and gradually evolving memory across a whole sequence
Yes, for most fixed-pattern recognition tasks on OHLCV windows
Reach for this specifically when evolving, long-range memory matters more than fixed local shapes

children.text: This chapter's closing case study builds an LSTM specifically for volatility forecasting on Nifty Bank, a reasonable choice given how strongly today's realized volatility depends on a gradually evolving memory of recent volatility, the well-documented volatility clustering effect behind GARCH-style models, rather than one fixed, short local shape. That said, the case study is a chance to apply this lesson's own advice: build the CNN version too, using it as the cheaper baseline the LSTM needs to beat, exactly the discipline Chapter 3's case study applied to stacking.

body.title: Computing a CNN's Receptive Field
body.prompt: A 1D CNN stacks 3 causal convolutional layers, each with kernel size 3, using dilation rates of 1, 2, and 4 respectively. Using Receptive Field = 1 + Σ(kernel size − 1) × dilation, what is the network's total receptive field, in time steps?
body.explanation: 1 + (3−1)×1 + (3−1)×2 + (3−1)×4 = 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15. Doubling the dilation rate at each layer, the same trick WaveNet popularized for audio, lets receptive field grow exponentially with depth instead of linearly, reaching 15 time steps with only 3 layers and a kernel size of 3.

body.title: Spotting a Non-Causal Convolution Leak
body.question: A 1D CNN for next-day direction prediction uses PyTorch's Conv1d with padding="same" and default, centered padding, applied directly to a price sequence ending on the prediction date. What is the most likely problem?
options: There is no problem; padding="same" just keeps the output length equal to the input length
The centered padding means each output position's receptive field includes input positions from both before and after it, letting future time steps leak into a prediction for an earlier date
Conv1d cannot be used on financial time series at all
The problem only occurs when the kernel size is even
body.explanation: A standard, centered convolution's output at position t depends on input positions both before and after t within its kernel width, the same shape of leak this course has flagged since Chapter 1, information from after the moment being predicted entering the prediction. A causal convolution, built by padding only on the left before applying the convolution with no additional padding, ensures the output at position t depends only on input positions at or before t.

points: A 1D convolution slides a weight-shared filter across time, detecting a local pattern regardless of where in the window it occurs, and processes all positions in parallel, typically training faster than an LSTM
Stacking dilated convolutional layers, with dilation doubling at each layer, grows the receptive field exponentially with depth, the technique WaveNet popularized for audio
A standard, centered convolution leaks future time steps into a prediction; a causal convolution, built with left-only padding, is required for any time series use
PyTorch's Conv1d with padding="same" is centered by default, not causal, making it an easy, framework-default leak to introduce by accident
CNNs are often the cheaper, faster first choice for fixed-length local pattern recognition; LSTMs earn their extra cost specifically when evolving, long-range memory genuinely matters

The chapter's case study builds an LSTM for volatility forecasting given volatility clustering's evolving-memory character, but a CNN baseline is still worth building alongside it, per this course's running rule that every model needs something simpler to beat
